title: Arakhin 6 - Borrowing from Charity Funds to Promote an Emergency Drive

chapters.title: Non-Jewish Donations to the Bet HaMikdash
chapters.about: Accepting gifts and building materials from non-Jews before and after construction.

chapters.title: Non-Jewish Terumah and God's Name on Items
chapters.about: Handling non-Jewish grain separation and removing sacred names for Geniza.

chapters.title: Borrowing from Charity Funds
chapters.about: Using charity money for personal needs and later replacing it with different coins.

chapters.title: Switching Dedicated Synagogue Items
chapters.about: Changing the use of donated candelabras for other mitzvah purposes.

chapters.title: Vows and Valuations for the Dying and Condemned
chapters.about: Arakhin and neder rules for individuals on their deathbed or facing execution.

chapters.title: Liability for Damages by the Condemned
chapters.about: Whether a person sentenced to death is liable for damages and if heirs must pay.

summary: This class explores laws regarding non-Jewish donations to the Bet HaMikdash and synagogues, the rules of borrowing and replacing money dedicated to charity (sedaka), and whether a person on their deathbed or facing execution can make vows or be held liable for damages. Rabbi Dr. Richard Hidary guides learners through the text of Masekhet Arakhin, analyzing opinions of early rabbinic authorities on temple construction, sacred names, and estate liabilities.
questions: Can a synagogue accept donations or building materials from non-Jews?
Is it permitted to borrow money that was already designated for charity and replace it later?
What happens when a non-Jew donates an item to a synagogue with God's name written on it?
Can someone on death row make a valuation vow (Arakhin) or be the object of one?
Do the heirs of a person sentenced to death have to pay for damages he caused before execution?
